title: binary heaps and priority queues
concepts: A priority queue exposes the highest- or lowest-priority element rather than insertion order; a binary heap is a common implementation, not the abstract contract itself.
A binary heap is a complete binary tree commonly stored in an array, with parent and child indices derived arithmetically and a heap-order invariant between each parent and child.
Insert restores heap order by sifting the new item upward; removal of the root replaces it with the final item and sifts downward.
A binary heap supports root peek in O(1) and insertion or root removal in O(log n); finding an arbitrary value is generally O(n) without an auxiliary index.
Bottom-up heap construction is O(n), which is asymptotically faster than inserting n elements one by one in O(n log n).
A min-heap and max-heap differ by priority ordering; a custom comparer can represent tuples or reverse priorities while requiring a consistent ordering.
Lazy deletion can leave stale entries in a heap and discard them when they reach the root; indexed heaps instead track positions to update or remove arbitrary entries.
A heap is useful for repeatedly selecting the next extremum, but sorted arrays, balanced trees, monotonic deques, or selection algorithms may fit other query patterns better.
